claim: Novel sensory experience increases NPAS4-positive neurons in CA1 from 3.4 ± 0.6% in standard environment to 11.2 ± 0.5% in enriched environment.
source: We observed a significant increase in NPAS4-positive neurons in CA1 from mice allowed to explore an EE relative to those maintained in an SE (Figure 1B and C; SE: 3.4 ± 0.6%, EE: 11.2 ± 0.5%; U=0, p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U Test)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunostaining data comparing NPAS4 expression between standard and enriched environments, with statistical analysis showing significant difference (p<0.001).

claim: NPAS4 protein is rapidly produced and degraded.
source: As NPAS4 protein is rapidly produced and degraded (Lin et al., 2008), this result probably significantly underestimates the percentage of neurons that expressed NPAS4 over the duration of the four days in EE.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2008.

claim: Experience-driven NPAS4 expression is similar among superficial and deep CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: We observed no significant effect of sublayer on NPAS4 expression as well as no significant interaction between CA1 sublayer and housing environment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Superficial EE: 11.3 ± 0.8% of neurons, Deep EE: 10.3 ± 1.0% of neurons, Sublayer: F(1,32)=1.86, p=0.18, Interaction: F(1,32)=0.04, p=0.84, two-way ANOVA), suggesting that experience-driven NPAS4 expression is similar among superficial and deep CA1 PNs.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data showing no significant difference in NPAS4 expression between superficial and deep CA1 sublayers (p=0.18), with statistical analysis using two-way ANOVA.

claim: Environmental enrichment increases somatic inhibitory synapses in wildtype but not Npas4 knockout hemispheres.
source: By contrast, and consistent with what has been described previously (Bloodgood et al., 2013), we detected a highly significant NPAS4-dependent increase in somatic inhibitory synapses in tissue from mice housed in EE (Figure 1E and F; WT: 277.3 ± 14.2 AU, KO: 209.4 ± 6.8 AU, p<0.001, two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc test).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing significant difference between WT and KO in enriched environment (p<0.001), and is also supported by citation to previous work (Bloodgood et al., 2013).

claim: The NPAS4-dependent increase in inhibitory synapses is significant only within superficial CA1, not deep CA1.
source: Surprisingly, analyzing superficial and deep sublayers in separate two-way ANOVAs revealed that the NPAS4-dependent increase in inhibitory synapses was significant only within superficial, and not deep, CA1, despite comparable experience-driven NPAS4 expression in both sublayers (Figure 1G; values for SE and EE, respectively: superficial – WT: 60.5 ± 4.5 AU, 107.8 ± 14.0 AU, KO: 57.8 ± 15.7 AU, 60.0 ± 7.7 AU, Genotype: F(1,37)=19.30, p<0.0001, Housing: F(1,37)=11.85, p=0.0014, Interaction: F(1,37)=17.78, p=0.0002; deep – WT: 147.5 ± 7.3 AU, 163.4 ± 8.7 AU, KO: 143.5 ± 5.4 AU, 157.2 ± 4.7 AU, Genotype: F(1,37)=1.89, p=0.18, Housing: F(1,37)=5.47, p=0.025, Interaction: F(1,37)=0.018, p=0.89, superficial WT vs KO for EE p<0.001, p>0.05 for all other comparisons, two-way ANOVAs with Bonferroni post hoc tests).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data with statistical analysis showing significant effects in superficial but not deep CA1.

claim: Housing mice in enriched environment results in larger evoked IPSCs in wildtype neurons relative to Npas4 knockout neurons in superficial CA1.
source: However, housing mice in an EE resulted in considerably larger eIPSCs in WT neurons relative to neighboring Npas4 KO neurons when the pair of PNs was localized to superficial CA1 (Figure 1I; WT: 1035.3 ± 196.9 pA, KO: 715.2 ± 116.1 pA, t=2.27, p=0.04, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing significant difference in eIPSC amplitudes between WT and KO neurons (p=0.04).

claim: No significant difference in evoked IPSC amplitude was measured between wildtype and Npas4 knockout neurons in deep CA1 from enriched mice.
source: No significant difference in eIPSC amplitude was measured when recording from neighboring WT and KO neurons in deep CA1 from enriched mice (Figure 1L; WT: 1146.4 ± 150.6 pA, KO: 1011.1 ± 194.5 pA, t=0.54, p=0.60, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing no significant difference (p=0.60) between WT and KO in deep CA1.

claim: Inhibition originating from CCKBCs is stronger onto superficial pyramidal neurons compared to deep CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Inhibition originating from CCKBCs is stronger onto superficial PNs in comparison to those in deep CA1 (Valero et al., 2015), while PVBCs more strongly inhibit PNs in deep CA1 (Lee et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Valero et al., 2015 and Lee et al., 2014.

claim: PVBCs more strongly inhibit pyramidal neurons in deep CA1.
source: Inhibition originating from CCKBCs is stronger onto superficial PNs in comparison to those in deep CA1 (Valero et al., 2015), while PVBCs more strongly inhibit PNs in deep CA1 (Lee et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2014.

claim: CCK- and PVBC synapses can be distinguished immunohistochemically via mutually exclusive expression of CB1R and parvalbumin, respectively.
source: Synapses that are made by CCK- and PVBCs can be distinguished immunohistochemically via the mutually exclusive expression of the presynaptic cannabinoid receptor (CB1R) and the calcium-binding protein parvalbumin (PV), respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the molecular markers that distinguish these cell types.

claim: Neither Cnr1 nor Pvalb genes appear to be direct targets of NPAS4.
source: Importantly, neither Cnr1 nor Pvalb genes, encoding CB1R or PV, respectively, appear to be direct targets of NPAS4 (Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2008.

claim: Only a fraction of CCK- and PV-expressing neurons induce NPAS4 in response to depolarization.
source: Furthermore, only a fraction of CCK- and PV-expressing neurons induce NPAS4 in response to depolarization (Spiegel et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Spiegel et al., 2014.

claim: Increased sensory experience associated with enriched environment leads to a significant increase in CCKBC synapse immunofluorescence in superficial CA1 from wildtype but not knockout hemispheres.
source: Increased sensory experience associated with EE, however, led to a significant increase in immunofluorescence in superficial CA1 from WT hemispheres that was not present in the KO hemispheres (Figure 2B and C; EE: superficial – WT: 159.51 ± 28.30 AU, KO: 67.87 ± 9.45 AU, p<0.001, two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing significant difference between WT and KO in enriched environment (p<0.001).

claim: No significant change in CCKBC synapse immunofluorescence was detected in deep CA1 between wildtype and knockout hemispheres in enriched environment.
source: No significant change was detected in deep CA1 (EE: deep – WT: 40.43 ± 3.38 AU, KO: 36.24 ± 3.05 AU, p>0.05, two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing no significant difference (p>0.05) in deep CA1.

claim: CCKBCs and PVBCs utilize distinct subtypes of voltage-gated calcium channels to trigger neurotransmitter release (N- and P/Q-type, respectively).
source: These cell types utilize distinct subtypes of voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) to trigger neurotransmitter release (N- and P/Q-type, respectively (Figure 2A) (Hefft and Jonas, 2005; Poncer et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hefft and Jonas, 2005 and Poncer et al., 1997.

claim: In superficial CA1 of mice from enriched environment, evoked IPSCs originating from CCKBCs were approximately 30% smaller in Npas4 knockout neurons than in neighboring wildtype neurons.
source: In superficial CA1 of mice from EE, eIPSCs originating from CCKBCs were ~30% smaller in Npas4 KO neurons than in neighboring WT neurons (Figure 2E; WT: 552.47 ± 104.75 pA, KO: 389. 80 ± 121.90 pA, W=84, p=0.032, Wilcoxon Signed-rank Test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data with pharmacological isolation of CCKBC transmission, showing significant difference (p=0.032).

claim: Housing mice in enriched environment significantly increased the normalized difference in CCKBC evoked IPSC amplitudes between wildtype and knockout pyramidal neurons in superficial CA1.
source: Importantly, housing mice in an EE significantly increased the normalized difference in CCKBC eIPSC amplitudes between WT and KO PNs in superficial CA1 relative to that seen in mice in SE (Figure 2F; SE: 0.081 ± 0.10, EE: 0.31 ± 0.07, t=1.18, p=0.041, unpaired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data comparing standard and enriched environments, showing significant difference (p=0.041).

claim: Novel sensory experiences drive an Npas4-dependent increase in CCKBC input onto pyramidal neurons in superficial CA1.
source: Thus, novel sensory experiences drive an Npas4-dependent increase in CCKBC input onto PNs in superficial CA1.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence including immunohistochemistry and electrophysiology data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No experience- or NPAS4-dependent change was detected in PVBC synapses visualized immunohistochemically.
source: We did not detect any experience- or NPAS4-dependent change in the PVBC synapses that were visualized immunohistochemically (Figure 3B and C; SE: superficial – WT: 53.68 ± 4.88 AU, KO: 56.34 ± 13.13 AU; deep – WT: 116.15 ± 9.31 AU, KO: 119.94 ± 5.85 AU; EE: superficial – WT: 55.76 ± 5.30 AU, KO: 54.86 ± 1.94 AU; deep – WT: 136.32 ± 8.25 AU, KO: 127.93 ± 14.02 AU; p>0.05 for all comparisons, two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing no significant differences (p>0.05) across all conditions.

claim: No difference in evoked IPSC amplitudes was observed between neighboring superficial Npas4 wildtype and knockout pyramidal neurons when transmission from PVBCs was pharmacologically isolated in mice from both standard and enriched environments.
source: Moreover, in mice from both SE and EE, we observed no difference in eIPSC amplitudes recorded from neighboring superficial Npas4 WT and KO PNs when transmission from PVCBs was pharmacologically isolated (Figure 3D and E; SE – WT: 554.5 ± 121.6 pA, KO: 655.7 ± 117.8 pA, t=0.84, p=0.43, paired t-test; EE– WT: 679.55 ± 150.68 pA, KO: 738.63 ± 179.41 pA, W=−13.00, p=0.65, Wilcoxon Signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data with pharmacological isolation showing no significant differences (p=0.43 for SE, p=0.65 for EE).

claim: Expression of NPAS4 in active CA1 pyramidal neurons leads to the selective increase of CCKBC inputs without significantly impacting PVBC synapses.
source: These results indicate that expression of NPAS4 in active CA1 PNs leads to the selective increase of CCKBC inputs without significantly impacting PVBC synapses.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental approaches including immunohistochemistry and electrophysiology comparing CCKBC and PVBC synapses.

claim: Significantly larger unitary IPSC amplitudes were recorded between CCKBC-pyramidal neuron pairs from mice in enriched environment relative to standard environment.
source: However, we recorded significantly larger uIPSC amplitudes between CCKBC–PN pairs from mice in EE relative to SE (Figure 4H and I; SE: 155.8 pA ± 27.83, EE: 450.6 pA ± 127.3, U=29.00, p=0.04, Mann-Whitney U Test).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired electrophysiological recordings showing significant difference (p=0.04) between environments.

claim: No difference in unitary IPSC amplitudes was measured between PVBC-pyramidal neuron pairs recorded in mice from standard versus enriched environment.
source: For PVBC–PN pairs, we measured no difference in uIPSC amplitudes recorded in mice from SE versus EE (Figure 4E and F; SE: 326.2 ± 131.1 pA, EE: 245.3 ± 76.86 pA, U=58.00, p=0.50, Mann-Whitney U Test).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired electrophysiological recordings showing no significant difference (p=0.50).

claim: Enriched environment drives the selective enhancement of synaptic input from individual CCKBCs onto individual superficial CA1 pyramidal neurons, without affecting inhibition from PVBCs.
source: Thus, EE drives the selective enhancement of synaptic input from individual CCKBCs onto individual superficial CA1 PNs, without affecting inhibition from PVBCs.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from paired recording data comparing CCKBC and PVBC inputs.

claim: Unitary IPSC amplitudes in wildtype pyramidal neurons were more than twice as large as those measured in Npas4 knockout pyramidal neurons in response to single action potentials evoked in a CCKBC.
source: On average, uIPSC amplitudes in WT PNs were more than twice as large as those measured in KO PNs (Figure 5C and D; WT: 450.64 ± 127.29 pA, KO: 183.97 ± 62.70 pA, U=29.00, p=0.044, Mann-Whitney U Test)
evidence: The claim is supported by paired electrophysiological recordings showing significant difference (p=0.044).

claim: NPAS4 increases the strength of individual CCKBC-pyramidal neuron connections.
source: On average, uIPSC amplitudes in WT PNs were more than twice as large as those measured in KO PNs (Figure 5C and D; WT: 450.64 ± 127.29 pA, KO: 183.97 ± 62.70 pA, U=29.00, p=0.044, Mann-Whitney U Test), demonstrating that NPAS4 increases the strength of individual CCKBC–PN connections.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from electrophysiological data showing larger uIPSC amplitudes in WT compared to KO neurons.

claim: The rise times and decay time constants of unitary IPSCs were indistinguishable between wildtype and Npas4 knockout pyramidal neurons.
source: Despite different uIPSC amplitudes, the rise times (10–90% of peak) and decay time constants (τ) of the currents were indistinguishable between the two genotypes (Figure 5D–F; rise time – WT: 1.13 ± 0.10 ms, KO: 1.06 ± 0.09 ms, t=0.44, p=0.67, unpaired t-test; τ – WT: 14.35 ± 0.83 ms, KO: 13.45 ± 1.01 ms, U=49.00, p=0.49, Mann-Whitney U Test)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements showing no significant differences (p=0.67 for rise time, p=0.49 for decay).

claim: Similar rise times and decay time constants suggest that synapses made onto wildtype and Npas4 knockout pyramidal neurons have similar postsynaptic receptor compositions.
source: Despite different uIPSC amplitudes, the rise times (10–90% of peak) and decay time constants (τ) of the currents were indistinguishable between the two genotypes (Figure 5D–F; rise time – WT: 1.13 ± 0.10 ms, KO: 1.06 ± 0.09 ms, t=0.44, p=0.67, unpaired t-test; τ – WT: 14.35 ± 0.83 ms, KO: 13.45 ± 1.01 ms, U=49.00, p=0.49, Mann-Whitney U Test), suggesting that the synapses made onto WT and KO PNs have similar postsynaptic receptor compositions (Gingrich et al., 1995; Lavoie and Twyman, 1996; Mody and Pearce, 2004; Thomson et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on electrophysiological data and supported by citations to literature on receptor kinetics.

claim: Unitary IPSCs recorded in Npas4 knockout pyramidal neurons had a significantly lower success rate than wildtype neurons.
source: Although there were few failures recorded in both genotypes, uIPSCs recorded in Npas4 KO PNs had a significantly lower success rate than did WT neurons (Figure 5G; WT: 0.94 ± 0.02, KO: 0.82 ± 0.04; U=22.00, p=0.01, Mann-Whitney U Test; 60–100 trials per connected pair, APs evoked at 0.1 Hz).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing significant difference in success rate (p=0.01).

claim: No effect of genotype on paired pulse ratios was detected at CCKBC synapses.
source: However, we detected no effect of genotype on PPRs as well as no interaction between genotype and PPR at various inter-spike-intervals (Figure 5H; 20 ms – WT: 0.81 ± 0.11, KO: 1.04 ± 0.18, 50 ms – WT: 0.85 ± 0.13, KO: 0.99 ± 0.12, 200 ms – WT: 0.83 ± 0.04, KO: 0.78 ± 0.10, and 1000 ms – WT: 0.94 ± 0.07, KO: 0.83 ± 0.17; Genotype: F(1,57)=0.77, p=0.39; Inter-spike-interval: F(3,57)=0.12, p=0.94; Interaction: F(3,57)=0.64, p=0.59)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing no significant effects (p=0.39 for genotype).

claim: The probability of release at individual CCKBC synapses made onto wildtype and Npas4 knockout neurons is unchanged.
source: However, we detected no effect of genotype on PPRs as well as no interaction between genotype and PPR at various inter-spike-intervals (Figure 5H; 20 ms – WT: 0.81 ± 0.11, KO: 1.04 ± 0.18, 50 ms – WT: 0.85 ± 0.13, KO: 0.99 ± 0.12, 200 ms – WT: 0.83 ± 0.04, KO: 0.78 ± 0.10, and 1000 ms – WT: 0.94 ± 0.07, KO: 0.83 ± 0.17; Genotype: F(1,57)=0.77, p=0.39; Inter-spike-interval: F(3,57)=0.12, p=0.94; Interaction: F(3,57)=0.64, p=0.59), suggesting that the probability of release at individual synapses made onto WT and KO neurons is unchanged.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on paired pulse ratio data showing no significant differences.

claim: The latency to unitary IPSC onset after action potential firing by the CCKBC was unchanged between wildtype and Npas4 knockout pyramidal neurons.
source: Similarly, the latency to uIPSC onset after AP firing by the CCKBC was unchanged between the two PN genotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; WT: 1.65 ± 0.12 ms, KO: 1.66 ± 0.17 ms, U=51.00, p=0.80, Mann-Whitney U Test)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing no significant difference (p=0.80).

claim: Unchanged latency to unitary IPSC onset provides further evidence for similar presynaptic organization between synapses converging on Npas4 wildtype and knockout neurons.
source: Similarly, the latency to uIPSC onset after AP firing by the CCKBC was unchanged between the two PN genotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; WT: 1.65 ± 0.12 ms, KO: 1.66 ± 0.17 ms, U=51.00, p=0.80, Mann-Whitney U Test), providing further evidence for similar presynaptic organization between synapses converging on Npas4 WT and KO neurons (Boudkkazi et al., 2007, 2011; Sabatini and Regehr, 1999).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on latency data and supported by citations to literature on presynaptic organization.

claim: An NPAS4-mediated increase in the number of contact sites made by individual CCKBCs onto pyramidal neurons is the most parsimonious mechanism to account for the lower success rate of unitary IPSCs in Npas4 knockout neurons.
source: If release probability at CCKBC synapses onto WT and KO neurons is indistinguishable, an NPAS4-mediated increase in the number of contact sites made by individual CCKBCs onto PNs is the most parsimonious mechanism to account for the lower success rate of uIPSCs in Npas4 KO neurons (Del Castillo and Katz, 1954).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combination of success rate and paired pulse ratio data, supported by citation to Del Castillo and Katz, 1954.

claim: The average coefficient of variation for wildtype pyramidal neurons was half that measured from Npas4 knockout neurons.
source: The average CV for WT PNs was half that measured from KO neurons (Figure 5J; WT: 44.17 ± 5.90, KO: 79.40 ± 9.80, t=3.199, p=0.005, unpaired t-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of coefficient of variation showing significant difference (p=0.005).

claim: The difference in unitary IPSC amplitudes between wildtype and Npas4 knockout neurons is due to a change in synapse number and unlikely to reflect differences in quantal amplitude.
source: The average CV for WT PNs was half that measured from KO neurons (Figure 5J; WT: 44.17 ± 5.90, KO: 79.40 ± 9.80, t=3.199, p=0.005, unpaired t-test), indicating that the difference in uIPSC amplitudes between WT and Npas4 KO neurons is due to a change in N and unlikely to reflect differences in Q (Berninger et al., 1999; Kerchner and Nicoll, 2008; Le Bé et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on coefficient of variation analysis and supported by citations to literature on quantal analysis.

claim: Variance-mean analysis of unitary IPSC amplitudes shows a linear relationship for both CCKBC-wildtype pyramidal neuron and CCKBC-knockout pyramidal neuron pairs.
source: Moreover, variance–mean analysis of uIPSC amplitudes shows a linear relationship for both CCKBC–WT PN and CCKBC–KO PN pairs (Figure 5K; WT: R2=0.89, KO: R2=0.84)
evidence: The claim is supported by variance-mean analysis showing high R-squared values for both genotypes.

claim: The linear fits of wildtype and knockout data sets are essentially superimposable, confirming that the probability of release is unchanged.
source: Strikingly, the linear fits of the WT and KO data sets are essentially superimposable (slope – WT: 55.55 ± 4.73, KO: 54.91 ± 5.46), confirming that the probability of release is unchanged and providing an indirect measurement of the quantal amplitude as ~55 pA in both genotypes (Reid and Clements, 1999).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on variance-mean analysis showing similar slopes, supported by citation to Reid and Clements, 1999.

claim: Asynchronous event amplitudes were comparable between wildtype and Npas4 knockout neurons.
source: These amplitudes were comparable between WT and KO neurons (Figure 5M; WT: 57.37 ± 3.62 pA, KO: 61.67 ± 6.50 pA, U=18.00, p=0.48, Mann-Whitney U Test)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements showing no significant difference (p=0.48).

claim: NPAS4 regulates the number of synapses made by an individual CCKBC onto a pyramidal neuron and does not significantly change the probability of release at individual synapses or the quantal amplitude.
source: Thus, we conclude that NPAS4 regulates the number of synapses made by an individual CCKBC onto a PN and does not significantly change the probability of release at individual synapses or the quantal amplitude.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including success rate, paired pulse ratio, coefficient of variation, variance-mean analysis, and asynchronous release measurements.

claim: Individual CCKBCs make, on average, eight synapses onto wildtype pyramidal neurons (range 1-29 synapses) and three onto Npas4 knockout neurons (range 1-13 synapses) in animals exposed to enriched environments.
source: On the basis of our measurements of Q and uIPSC amplitudes, individual CCKBCs make, on average, eight synapses onto WT (1–29 synapses) and three onto Npas4 KOs neurons (1–13 synapses) in animals exposed to enriched environments.
evidence: The claim is a calculation based on measured quantal amplitude and unitary IPSC amplitudes.

claim: Membrane depolarization triggers the production of endocannabinoids by pyramidal neurons, which act retrogradely by binding presynaptic CB1Rs, resulting in the transient suppression of inhibitory transmission (DSI).
source: Membrane depolarization triggers the production of endocannabinoids by PNs, which act retrogradely by binding presynaptic CB1Rs, resulting in the transient suppression of inhibitory transmission (DSI) (Wilson and Nicoll, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wilson and Nicoll, 2001.

claim: CCKBCs are notable for their expression of CB1Rs and for their cannabinoid-mediated plasticity.
source: CCKBCs are notable for their expression of CB1Rs and for their cannabinoid-mediated plasticity (Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006.

claim: Housing mice in enriched environment resulted in a nearly two-fold increase in DSI magnitude relative to standard environment in wildtype pyramidal neurons.
source: Notably, housing mice in EE resulted in a nearly two-fold increase in DSI magnitude relative to SE in WT PNs (Figure 6B and C, DSI magnitude in WT – SE: 26 ± 7%, EE: 48 ± 4%, p<0.05, two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of DSI showing significant difference (p<0.05).

claim: The magnitude of DSI measured in Npas4 knockout pyramidal neurons from mice living in standard and enriched environments was comparable to that measured in wildtype pyramidal neurons from mice in standard environment.
source: Indeed, the magnitude of DSI measured in Npas4 KO PNs from mice living in SE and EE was comparable to that measured in WT PNs from mice in SE (Figure 6B and C; DSI magnitude, KO – SE: 31 ± 6%, EE: 29 ± 5%, EE WT vs EE KO p<0.05, two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc test)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements showing no significant difference between KO neurons in SE and EE, but significant difference between WT and KO in EE (p<0.05).

claim: DSI was completely prevented by bath application of the CB1R antagonist AM251.
source: Finally, DSI was completely prevented by bath application of the CB1R antagonist AM251 (Figure 6B and C; DSI magnitude, WT: 3 ± 7%, KO: 3 ± 1%, WT baseline integrated current vs integrated current after DSI: W=−26.00, p=0.28, Mann-Whitney U Test; KO baseline integrated current vs integrated current after DSI: W=9.00, p=0.65, Mann-Whitney U Test), confirming that this effect is due to endocannabinoid-mediated DSI.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation showing elimination of DSI with CB1R antagonist.

claim: NPAS4 enhances endocannabinoid-mediated plasticity in CA1 of the hippocampus.
source: Together, our results support a model of experience-dependent regulation of CCKBC synapses by postsynaptic NPAS4 expression, and demonstrate that NPAS4 enhances endocannabinoid-mediated plasticity in CA1 of the hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from DSI experiments showing enhanced DSI in WT neurons from enriched environment.

claim: NPAS4 is expressed exclusively in response to membrane depolarization.
source: The IEG-TF neuronal PAS domain protein 4 (NPAS4) is expressed exclusively in response to membrane depolarization (Lin et al., 2008), explicitly linking this expression to the activity history of the neuron.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2008.

claim: Behaviorally induced NPAS4 directs the reorganization of inhibition along the somato-dendritic axis of hippocampal pyramidal neurons, enhancing somatic inhibition and reducing inhibition in the proximal dendrites.
source: Behaviorally induced NPAS4 directs the reorganization of inhibition along the somato-dendritic axis of hippocampal pyramidal neurons (PNs), enhancing somatic inhibition and reducing inhibition in the proximal dendrites (Bloodgood et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bloodgood et al., 2013.

claim: Fast-spiking PVBCs provide reliable, precisely timed neurotransmission in response to predominantly feedforward synaptic input.
source: Fast-spiking PVBCs provide reliable, precisely timed neurotransmission in response to predominantly feedforward synaptic input (Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006), positioning them to finely regulate the timing of PN action potential (AP) firing (Pouille and Scanziani, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006 and Pouille and Scanziani, 2001.

claim: PVBCs finely regulate the timing of pyramidal neuron action potential firing.
source: Fast-spiking PVBCs provide reliable, precisely timed neurotransmission in response to predominantly feedforward synaptic input (Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006), positioning them to finely regulate the timing of PN action potential (AP) firing (Pouille and Scanziani, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pouille and Scanziani, 2001.

claim: CCKBCs elicit slower and less reliable, asynchronous inhibition in response to the summation of both feedforward and feedback synaptic input.
source: By contrast, CCKBCs elicit slower and less reliable, asynchronous inhibition (Daw et al., 2009; Hefft and Jonas, 2005) in response to the summation of both feedforward and feedback synaptic input (Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Daw et al., 2009, Hefft and Jonas, 2005, and Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006.

claim: CCKBCs express a variety of neuromodulatory receptors, including cannabinoid receptors (CB1Rs) that are localized to their axon terminals.
source: Importantly, CCKBCs express a variety of neuromodulatory receptors, including cannabinoid receptors (CB1Rs) that are localized to their axon terminals (Dudok et al., 2015; Glickfeld et al., 2008; Katona et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dudok et al., 2015, Glickfeld et al., 2008, and Katona et al., 1999.

claim: Activation of CCKBC CB1Rs by endocannabinoids, which are released from postsynaptic pyramidal neurons, underlies depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition (DSI).
source: Indeed, activation of CCKBC CB1Rs by endocannabinoids, which are released from postsynaptic PNs, underlies depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition (DSI) (Wilson and Nicoll, 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wilson and Nicoll, 2001.

claim: DSI is a form of retrograde signaling that confers onto active pyramidal neurons a transient window of increased excitability and plasticity.
source: Indeed, activation of CCKBC CB1Rs by endocannabinoids, which are released from postsynaptic PNs, underlies depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition (DSI) (Wilson and Nicoll, 2001), a form of retrograde signaling that confers onto active PNs a transient window of increased excitability and plasticity (Carlson et al., 2002; Chevaleyre and Castillo, 2004; Zhu and Lovinger, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carlson et al., 2002, Chevaleyre and Castillo, 2004, and Zhu and Lovinger, 2007.

claim: Activity-driven NPAS4 expression increases somatic inhibition onto pyramidal neurons.
source: Activity-driven NPAS4 expression increases somatic inhibition onto PNs, but it is unknown whether this synaptic regulation is interneuron subtype-specific.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, setting up the research question.

claim: Novel sensory experiences selectively increase the number of inhibitory synapses made by individual CCKBCs onto CA1 pyramidal neurons through an NPAS4-dependent mechanism.
source: Using behavioral manipulations in combination with electrophysiological, pharmacological, and anatomical approaches, we show that novel sensory experiences selectively increase the number of inhibitory synapses made by individual CCKBCs onto CA1 PNs through an NPAS4-dependent mechanism.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings from multiple experimental approaches presented in the manuscript.

claim: Experience-driven NPAS4 expression strongly enhances DSI expression by active pyramidal neurons.
source: Moreover, we find that this interneuron subtype-specific circuit change strongly enhances DSI expression by active PNs.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the DSI findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Abnormal wiring of CCK inhibitory neurons disrupts the spatial coherence of place fields.
source: Indeed, abnormal wiring of CCK inhibitory neurons disrupts the spatial coherence of place fields (Del Pino et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Del Pino et al., 2017.

claim: The opposing gradients of inhibition from PV- and CCKBCs along the superficial to deep axis of the hippocampus underlies the heterogeneity of pyramidal neuron spiking associated with sharp wave ripples.

claim: Superficial and deep CA1 pyramidal neurons form separate microcircuits.
source: Thus NPAS4 likely enhances the gradient of CCKBC inhibition along the superficial to deep axis, and our finding reinforces the idea that superficial and deep CA1 PNs form separate microcircuits (Danielson et al., 2016; Geiller et al., 2017).

claim: NPAS4 likely enhances the gradient of CCKBC inhibition along the superficial to deep axis.
source: Thus NPAS4 likely enhances the gradient of CCKBC inhibition along the superficial to deep axis, and our finding reinforces the idea that superficial and deep CA1 PNs form separate microcircuits (Danielson et al., 2016; Geiller et al., 2017).

claim: The formation of CCKBC synapses relies on postsynaptic expression of the dystroglycan complex.
source: Recent work has revealed that the formation of CCKBC synapses relies on postsynaptic expression of the dystroglycan complex (Früh et al., 2016), whereas formation of PVBC synapses does not.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Früh et al., 2016.

claim: Dystroglycans and associated proteins are compelling candidates through which NPAS4 may regulate CCKBC synapses.
source: Dystroglycans, and the proteins that associate with them, are compelling candidates through which NPAS4 may regulate CCKBC synapses, although others may yet be identified.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the finding that NPAS4 specifically regulates CCKBC synapses and the known role of dystroglycans in CCKBC synapse formation.

claim: DSI of CCKBC synapses can facilitate the induction of long-term potentiation in pyramidal neurons.
source: As DSI of CCKBC synapses can also facilitate the induction of long-term potentiation (LTP) in PNs (Carlson et al., 2002), this window of disinhibition may facilitate LTP at inputs active during DSI and help to coordinate the plasticity of common inputs to NPAS4-expressing neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Carlson et al., 2002.

claim: A function of NPAS4 expression may be to increase the signal and reduce the noise within the local microcircuit by refining pyramidal neuron firing.
source: More broadly, a function of NPAS4 expression may be to increase the signal and reduce the noise within the local microcircuit by refining PN firing (Bartos and Elgueta, 2012).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental findings and supported by citation to Bartos and Elgueta, 2012.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in which NPAS4 is expressed will be subject to enhanced CCKBC inhibition, thus reducing CA1 pyramidal neuron spiking during low to moderate network activity.
source: For example, our data imply that PNs in which NPAS4 is expressed will be subject to enhanced CCKBC inhibition, thus reducing CA1 PN spiking during low to moderate network activity.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference from the experimental findings about increased CCKBC synapses.

claim: When pyramidal neuron activity levels surpass the threshold for triggering cannabinoid production, a temporal window will open in which the pyramidal neuron can disinhibit itself, generate more action potentials, and lower the threshold for plasticity.
source: However, when PN activity levels surpass the threshold for triggering cannabinoid production, leading to the temporary suppression of transmission from CCKBCs through DSI, a temporal window will open in which the PN can disinhibit itself, generate more APs, and lower the threshold for plasticity.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference from the experimental findings about enhanced DSI.

claim: NPAS4 has been reported to decrease inhibitory synapses in the proximal apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: The current study describes a role for NPAS4 in regulating somatic inhibition specifically provided by CCKBCs to superficial CA1 PNs, however NPAS4 has also been reported to decrease inhibitory synapses in the proximal apical dendrites of CA1 PNs (Bloodgood et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bloodgood et al., 2013.

claim: CCK inhibitory neurons are a heterogeneous population comprised of basket cells and dendrite-targeting cells including Schaffer collateral-associated and perforant path-associated inhibitory neurons.
source: CCK inhibitory neurons are themselves a heterogeneous population of neurons in CA1, comprised of basket cells and dendrite-targeting cells including Schaffer collateral-associated (SCA) and perforant path-associated inhibitory neurons (Booker et al., 2017; Cope et al., 2002; Klausberger et al., 2005; Pawelzik et al., 2002; Vida et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Booker et al., 2017, Cope et al., 2002, Klausberger et al., 2005, Pawelzik et al., 2002, and Vida et al., 1998.

claim: CCKBCs generate significant asynchronous release, which is quantal in nature.

claim: Recent studies indicate functional distinctions between pyramidal neurons in the superficial and deep sublayers of CA1.
source: Recent studies indicate functional distinctions between PNs in the superficial (closest to stratum radiatum, SR) and deep (closest to stratum oriens, SO) sublayers of CA1 (Geiller et al., 2017), including gene expression profiles (Cembrowski et al., 2016), firing patterns (Baimbridge et al., 1991), and connectivity with excitatory (Masurkar et al., 2017) and inhibitory neurons (Lee et al., 2014; Valero et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Geiller et al., 2017, Cembrowski et al., 2016, Baimbridge et al., 1991, Masurkar et al., 2017, Lee et al., 2014, and Valero et al., 2015.
